grammar: 行くわよ uses わよ — a feminine assertive/decisive sentence ending. Here Lulu uses the plain non-volitional form 行く with わよ to declare action, rather than 行こう (let's go). The plain present with わよ can carry a commanding, 'we're going now' nuance.

text: 乗り込むわよ
translation: We're storming in!

vocabulary.meaning: to board, to storm into, to charge in

grammar: 乗り込む has a nuance of forceful entry — not just 'getting on' but barging in. わよ again marks Lulu's decisive, commanding feminine speech. The repetition from clip_219 reinforces that the rescue attempt is now actually underway.

text: スピラに来てすぐにアルベト族に助けてもらったんだ
translation: Right when I got to Spira, the Al Bhed helped me out.

vocabulary.meaning: to be helped by, to receive help from

grammar: 〜てもらう expresses receiving a favor or action from someone — 助けてもらった means 'they helped me (and I benefitted).' This is distinct from 助けてくれた (they helped me) — もらう emphasizes the speaker's receiving perspective. んだ adds explanation/context.

text: 船に乗せてもらって飯も食わせてもらったし
translation: They let me ride on their ship and even gave me food.

vocabulary.meaning: to be given a ride, to have someone let you ride
to be fed, to have someone give you food
and (listing reasons or facts, implying there's more)

grammar: 〜てもらって connects two receiving-of-favor actions: 乗せてもらって (was let ride) and 食わせてもらった (was fed). 〜し at the end lists examples with the implication of 'among other things.' 食わせる is the causative of 食う — 'to make someone eat / to feed someone.'

text: その時の船かなって思ったんだけど
translation: I thought maybe it was that ship from back then.

vocabulary.meaning: I wonder if, maybe (expressing mild uncertainty)

grammar: 〜かなって思った is a common structure: かな (wondering/maybe) + って (quotation) + 思った (thought). It captures internal tentative wondering: 'I kinda thought maybe...' んだけど trails off, implying the next line contradicts or qualifies the thought.

text: 違うみたいだ
translation: But it seems like it's not.

vocabulary.meaning: to differ, to be wrong, not to be (the case)
it seems like, it appears to be

grammar: みたいだ is a colloquial evidential marker expressing inference from observation — 'it seems/appears (based on what I see).' More casual than ようだ. 違う here means 'it's different / it's not that ship.'

text: みんなやられちまったのかな / 何かあったの?
translation: I wonder if they all got done in / Did something happen?

vocabulary.meaning: to be beaten, to be done in, to be attacked (passive/resultative)
ended up (doing), unfortunately did (casual contraction of 〜てしまった)

grammar: やられちまった is a contraction of やられてしまった — the てしまう form expresses an undesirable completed action ('ended up being beaten'). のかな is a wondering sentence ending — のか (explanatory question) + な (mild wondering) = 'I wonder if that's what happened.'

text: 船の近くにシンが出たんだ / 俺は助かったけど船はどうなったかわからない
translation: Sin appeared near the ship / I survived, but I don't know what happened to the ship.

vocabulary.meaning: to appear, to come out, to show up
to be saved, to survive, to escape danger
what became of, what happened to

grammar: 〜んだ explains or gives context: 'the thing is, Sin appeared.' 助かったけど uses けど (but) to contrast Tidus's survival with uncertainty about the ship. どうなったかわからない embeds a question: 'I don't know [what happened to it].'

text: あのさ、その船にシドって人いなかった?
translation: Hey, was there someone named Cid on that ship?

vocabulary.meaning: was not there, was not present (past negative of いる)

grammar: いなかった? with rising intonation turns the negative past into a question: 'wasn't there someone...?' This is more tentative than いた? (was there?) — Yuna isn't sure if Cid was there and is asking with some uncertainty. あのさ is a soft, casual conversation opener.

text: わかんないな、言葉も通じなかったしさ
translation: I don't know, the language didn't get through either.

vocabulary.meaning: don't know (casual contraction of わからない)
to get through, to be understood, to communicate

grammar: 言葉も通じなかった — も (even/also) here adds: 'the language didn't get through either' (on top of everything else). しさ is a casual trailing ending: し (listing reason) + さ (softener/filler). The combination is very colloquial male speech.

text: そっか / その人知り合い?
translation: I see / Is that person someone you know?

vocabulary.meaning: I see, oh really (casual contraction of そうか)

grammar: そっか is a very casual acknowledgment (そうか → そっか), expressing that the speaker has taken in the new information. 知り合い? as a lone question-word sentence is a fragment — casual speech drops the full predicate (知り合いですか or 知り合いなの?).

text: おじさんなの、会ったことはないけど
translation: He's my uncle, though I've never met him.
grammar: なの is the explanatory copula (な + の) in a feminine/soft register. 会ったことはない uses こと (nominalizer) to describe a past experience: 'the experience of having met.' は adds contrastive nuance: 'I haven't met him, but (he's family).'

text: ふーん
translation: Hmm.

vocabulary.meaning: hmm, I see (neutral acknowledgment with mild interest or slight surprise)

grammar: ふーん is a non-verbal filler of acknowledgment. Unlike そうか (understanding) or へえ (surprise), ふーん is more neutral — processing information without strong reaction. It can also subtly signal that the speaker is thinking.

text: あれ?ってことは、ユーナもアルベド族?
translation: Wait — does that mean Yuna is Al Bhed too?

vocabulary.meaning: huh? wait a moment (interjection of sudden realization)
in other words, that means, so (logical inference)

grammar: ってことは is a colloquial connector meaning 'that means' or 'so that implies' — Tidus is drawing an inference. あれ? marks a sudden realization or puzzlement. The sentence ends without a verb (ユーナもアルベド族?), which is a casual question by omission.

text: お母さんがね、そうなの。シドさんはお母さんのお兄さん。お母さんが結婚するときに縁を切ったんだって。
translation: My mother is, yes. Cid is my mother's older brother. Apparently they cut ties when my mother got married.

vocabulary.meaning: to cut ties, to sever a relationship

grammar: ね after お母さんがね softens the sentence and creates a pause for emotional weight. んだって marks hearsay — Yuna is reporting something she was told, not something she witnessed. This distinguishes it from んだ (direct explanation) — here it means 'I was told that they cut ties.'

text: でも、困ったときには相談しなさいってお母さんが。
translation: But my mother said to consult him when I'm in trouble.

vocabulary.meaning: to be troubled, to be in a fix, to have trouble
to consult, to talk over, to seek advice

grammar: 〜ときには: 〜とき (when) + は (topic/emphasis) — 'when in trouble, specifically.' 相談しなさい is a mild imperative often used by parents/superiors. って at the end marks it as a quote from お母さん. The trailing が leaves the sentence open: 'my mother (said so)' — the verb of speaking is implied.

text: そりゃ心配だよな。 / ユーナの生まれのことは、輪っかには言わないで。あの人、アルベド族ってだけでけぎらしてるから。
translation: That must be worrying. / Don't tell Wakka about Yuna's birth. That person prejudges just because someone is Al Bhed.

vocabulary.meaning: that is, of course, naturally (casual contraction of それは)
prejudice, dislike based on appearance alone (毛嫌い)

grammar: だよな uses な to seek shared understanding/agreement: 'that's worrying, right?' 〜ないで is a negative request/command: 'don't tell.' あの人, アルベド族ってだけで — 'just because (they are) Al Bhed' — ってだけで emphasizes the sole basis for Wakka's prejudice. けぎらいしてる (毛嫌いしている) means blanket rejection based on surface impression.

text: ああ!わっかに散らせなくちゃ! / 「わっかには内緒に」って言ったじゃない!
translation: Oh! I have to tell Wakka! / I told you to keep it secret from Wakka!

vocabulary.meaning: (here, likely) to tell, to spread (possibly mishearing/mistaking 知らせる = to inform)
must do, have to (casual contraction of 〜なくてはならない)
I told you, didn't I? (reproaching reminder)

grammar: なくちゃ is a strong contraction of なくてはいけない (must do). 言ったじゃない is a reproachful reminder — 'didn't I say?' / 'I told you, didn't I?' じゃない at sentence-end with falling intonation expresses mild accusation or exasperation, not a genuine question.

text: 試合!
translation: The match!
grammar: A single-word exclamation — someone shouting as a reminder that the blitzball final is about to start. Full sentence omitted in the urgency of the moment.

text: おっと!残り時間30秒! オーラかステミノ全員攻撃だ!
translation: Oh! 30 seconds remaining! The Aurochs are all-out attacking!
grammar: Broadcast commentary style — short, punchy sentences. 全員攻撃だ uses だ for declarative assertion: 'it's an all-member attack!' 残り時間30秒 is a noun phrase without a verb — typical of urgent announcements where copulas are dropped for speed.

text: ネッティからのロングパース! / 通ったぞ!
translation: A long pass from Letty! / It went through!

vocabulary.meaning: to pass through, to get through

grammar: 〜からのロングパース — からの is a nominalizing construction: 'a long pass from Netty.' This is a common sportscaster structure. 通ったぞ uses ぞ for excited exclamation — the pass made it! ぞ is masculine and emphatic, fitting for broadcast excitement.

text: シュート!
translation: Shoot!
grammar: Single-word exclamation from the commentator or crowd, marking the moment of the shot attempt.

text: ゴール!
translation: Goal!
grammar: Celebratory exclamation — the universal sports shout, borrowed directly from English.

text: リサイドオラカ!3対2で奇跡の勝利です!
translation: The Besaid Aurochs! A miraculous victory, 3 to 2!
grammar: 3対2 (さんたいに) is the score format: 'three to two.' 奇跡の勝利 uses の to connect noun + noun: 'a victory of miracles / a miraculous victory.' です makes it polite broadcast speech.

text: 勝った! / やった!次は決勝!
translation: We won! / Yes! Next is the final!
grammar: 勝った is the plain past of 勝つ used as an exclamation. やった is literally 'did it!' — past tense of やる used as a fixed celebratory expression. 次は決勝! drops the verb — 'Next is the final!' spoken in the heat of excitement.

text: 勝てたからいいけど、カッコつかないわね。
translation: We won so it's fine, but it wasn't very cool.

vocabulary.meaning: managed to win (potential past of 勝つ)
not cool, not stylish, lacking dignity (カッコ=格好)

grammar: 勝てたからいいけど — potential past 勝てた + から (since/because) + いいけど (it's fine, but). The けど (but) introduces the qualification. わね is a feminine sentence-final particle combining わ (assertion) and ね (seeking agreement) — Lulu's characteristically measured critique.

text: チャップなら最後までちゃんとしてたの。
translation: Chappu would have done it properly right to the end.

vocabulary.meaning: if it were 〜, in the case of 〜 (conditional)
until the end, right through to the last
to do properly, to do correctly

grammar: チャップなら is a counterfactual conditional — 'if it were Chappu / if it had been Chappu.' This implies comparison and regret. してたの uses の at the end in a feminine explanatory tone, and してた (was doing) implies a sustained state: Chappu would have stayed composed throughout.

text: あって?そういうこと言っていいわけ?
translation: Hey? Is it okay to say something like that?

vocabulary.meaning: that kind of thing, something like that
is it okay to say, is saying it alright

grammar: 〜ていいわけ? is a casual inquiry challenging permissibility — 言っていい (it's okay to say) + わけ? (is that the case? / is that really okay?). わけ as a question particle pushes for justification: 'does that mean you're allowed to say that?' Tidus is calling out Lulu for bringing up Chappu.

text: 突然、何?
translation: Suddenly, what?
grammar: A two-word fragment — Lulu responding with mock or genuine surprise: 'What are you saying out of nowhere?' The verb is dropped entirely. 突然 + 何 is a shorthand challenge: 'where is this coming from?'

text: 俺はチャップの代わりにはなれない / ワッカにそう言ってくれたのはルルだろう
translation: I can't be a replacement for Chappu / Wasn't it you, Lulu, who told Wakka that?

vocabulary.meaning: told (someone, doing a favor for them)

grammar: 〜の代わりには marks the role being rejected: 'in the role of replacement for.' には adds contrastive/emphatic nuance. 言ってくれたのはルルだろう uses の nominalization + だろう (right?) as a rhetorical confirmation: 'it was you who told him, wasn't it?'

text: ワッカだってチャップの代わりなんか / 最後まで言ったら怒るわよ
translation: If you say that Wakka is just Chappu's replacement, all the way to the end / I'll get angry.
grammar: The sentence is left incomplete intentionally — 最後まで言ったら (if you say it all the way to the end) + 怒るわよ (I'll get angry). This mimics cutting Tidus off before he can finish the thought. Lulu warns him not to complete the sentence. わよ adds assertive feminine emphasis.

text: ワッカさん大丈夫ですか?
translation: Are you alright, Wakka?
grammar: Standard polite inquiry using ですか. Tidus uses the polite suffix さん and ですか, showing respect toward Wakka as a senior player/guardian. The shift to polite register mirrors Tidus checking in on someone he cares about.

text: もうすぐ決勝が始まるってのに / この怪我じゃ…
translation: The final is about to start, and yet / with this injury…

vocabulary.meaning: even though, and yet (expressing frustration at a contradiction)

grammar: 〜ってのに (contraction of というのに) expresses frustrated contradiction: 'even though the final is about to start.' この怪我じゃ... is an incomplete sentence trailing off — じゃ (short for では) introduces a condition: 'with this injury, (I can't...).' The ellipsis conveys Wakka's despair.

text: 相手はゴアーズだし…
translation: And the opponent is the Goers on top of that…

vocabulary.meaning: and (on top of that), what's more (listing compounding reasons)

grammar: だし adds another item to a list of problems — 'the injury, and also the opponent is the Goers.' The trailing ellipsis (…) marks the sentence as incomplete, conveying Wakka's sense of hopelessness without stating it directly.

text: 待たせたな!
translation: Sorry to keep you waiting!

vocabulary.meaning: to make someone wait (causative of 待つ)

grammar: 待たせたな is the plain past causative of 待つ + な (soft acknowledgment/mild regret). The full version would be 待たせてしまった (I made you wait) but the truncated form is more casual and energetic — Yuna returning after being rescued, acknowledging the concern caused without dwelling on it.

text: ユーナさん! / 怪我ないっすか?
translation: Yuna! / Are you not injured?

vocabulary.meaning: isn't there? / you don't have any, right? (polite-casual negative question)

grammar: 怪我ないっすか? — 怪我ない (no injury) + っすか (polite-casual question suffix). This is a concern-check: 'You aren't hurt, are you?' The polite っす here is Tidus's way of being respectful to Yuna while remaining casual.

text: 心配かけちゃって…
translation: I'm sorry for worrying you…

vocabulary.meaning: to cause worry, to make someone worry
ended up (doing) — remorseful or regretful (casual contraction of 〜てしまって)

grammar: 心配かけちゃって is short for 心配をかけてしまって (having caused worry — regretfully). The trailing て form without a main clause is an apology fragment: 'for having caused worry...' — the unspoken implication is 'I'm sorry.' This structure conveys guilt through incompleteness.

text: ごめんなさい!ごめんなさい!ごめんなさい!
translation: I'm sorry! I'm sorry! I'm sorry!
grammar: Repetition of ごめんなさい three times indicates extreme remorse or distress. The tripling is an emotional intensifier — Yuna is genuinely distraught, not giving a casual apology.

text: なんだってアルベドなんかに連れて行かれるんだよ
translation: Why on earth did you let yourself get taken by the Al Bhed?

vocabulary.meaning: why on earth, how could it be that (indignant question)
to be taken, to be led away (passive of 連れて行く)

grammar: なんだって + 〜んだよ is an exasperated rhetorical question: 'How could you...?' んだよ adds emotional weight and demands explanation. アルベドなんかに uses なんか dismissively — 'people like the Al Bhed.' 連れて行かれる is passive: Yuna was 'led away.'

text: もうその話はいいだろ?
translation: That's enough of that, right?

vocabulary.meaning: that's fine / that's enough, right? (seeking agreement)

grammar: もう〜はいい is a fixed expression: 'enough of 〜, that's enough.' だろ (casual form of だろう) seeks agreement: 'right?' or 'don't you think?' Tidus is trying to cut off Wakka's scolding of Yuna.

text: もうアルベドとは口聞くなよ / 面倒に巻き込まれっからな
translation: Don't talk to the Al Bhed anymore / You'll get dragged into trouble.

vocabulary.meaning: to talk (to someone), to speak with
to be dragged in, to get involved (passive of 巻き込む)

grammar: 口聞くなよ — 聞くな is the negative imperative of 聞く (don't), and よ softens the command slightly while keeping it firm. 巻き込まれっから (contraction of 巻き込まれるから) — 'because you'll get dragged in.' Wakka's prejudice and protectiveness both on display here.

text: もうすぐ決勝戦スタートだ / ウォーミングアップしてる時間はねえ
translation: The final match is about to start / There's no time for warming up.

vocabulary.meaning: there's no time (colloquial: ねえ = ない)

grammar: スタートだ uses だ for blunt declaration. ねえ is a colloquial/masculine form of ない — 'there isn't.' 時間はねえ is colloquially forceful: 'there's just no time.' The は adds contrast: 'for warming up specifically, there's no time.'

text: いけるか / 余裕っす
translation: Can you do it? / No problem.

vocabulary.meaning: can do it, good to go, manageable
composure, room to spare, no problem, easy

grammar: いけるか is a casual question (potential form + か): 'Can you manage?' 余裕っす is a very confident response — 余裕 (room to spare, no sweat) + っす (polite-casual suffix). Tidus is projecting confidence before the final.

text: 今のうちに言っとくことがある
translation: There's something I need to say while I have the chance.

vocabulary.meaning: while there's still time, while I have the chance
to say in advance, to tell beforehand (contraction of 言っておく)

grammar: 今のうちに marks urgency: 'while there's still opportunity.' 言っとく is a casual contraction of 言っておく (〜ておく = to do in advance/leave it said). 〜ことがある means 'there is something that...' — here it means 'there is something I must say.' Wakka's serious tone signals a significant announcement.

text: 決勝戦が終わったら / 俺は
translation: When the final match is over / I…

vocabulary.meaning: when it ends, once it is over (conditional)

grammar: 〜たら is a conditional/temporal: 'when/once 〜 ends.' The sentence is deliberately cut off after 俺は — building suspense before the revelation in the next clip. 俺は sets up the subject 'I' with は emphasizing it as the topic of the announcement.

text: 引退する
translation: I'm retiring.
grammar: A single verb — the delayed revelation after the pause in clip_271. The plain non-past 引退する (not 引退します) suggests this is not a polite announcement but a firm, personal declaration. The brevity is intentional — the weight of the word speaks for itself.

text: この大会が最後だって / 前から決めてたからな
translation: I had decided this tournament would be my last / I decided that a long time ago.

vocabulary.meaning: from before, for a long time now
had decided (casual past progressive of 決める)

grammar: だって quotes his own prior decision: 'I had decided that this tournament would be the last.' 前から indicates the decision was made well in advance. 決めてたからな — から explains the reason, な adds a reflective masculine softener: 'because I'd already decided, you see.'

text: 結果は関係ねえ / 勝っても負けても引退だ
translation: The result doesn't matter / Win or lose, I'm retiring.

vocabulary.meaning: doesn't matter, is irrelevant (colloquial: ねえ = ない)

vocabulary.reading: かっても まけても

grammar: 〜ても〜ても is a double concessive structure: 'even if A, even if B' = 'regardless of A or B.' 勝っても負けても = 'whether we win or lose.' 関係ねえ is colloquial male speech for 関係ない. 引退だ with だ is a definitive statement — this is Wakka's resolute final declaration.
